summary.title: You Want Microservices—But Do You Need Them?
summary.one_liner: Microservices add operational, testing, and data-consistency costs that most teams don't need to pay, so a modular monolith or SOA is often the better default unless you operate at very large scale.
takeaways: Microservices trade a single codebase's simplicity for network calls, service discovery, tracing, and version management, which adds cost and failure points.
Case studies from Amazon Prime Video, Twilio Segment and Shopify show teams reversing or avoiding microservices to cut cost and complexity.
Microservices justify themselves mainly when distinct business capabilities need independent scaling and deployment, and when team structure matches the boundaries.
Modular monoliths (for most applications and startups) and SOA (for enterprises) offer comparable scalability with stronger consistency and simpler debugging.
Docker can package and scale a monolith consistently, so containerization does not require adopting microservices.
summary.summary: The article argues that microservices are often adopted by default rather than because requirements justify them. It weighs the agility benefits against hidden costs: operational overhead, slower and more brittle testing, developer productivity drag, and the difficulty of data consistency across service boundaries. It supports the argument with reversal stories from Amazon Prime Video, Twilio Segment and Shopify, and quotes from figures such as DHH, Jason Warner, Nick Schrock, Gergely Orosz and Kelsey Hightower. It then presents modular monoliths and SOA as alternatives and closes with a promotional section on how Docker supports any architecture, including a containerized monolith.
